rationale: B wins because it is the cleaner strategist: it keeps the money story tight and makes the missing proof explicit instead of sneaking speculation into the headline. Its best line, "whether charging margin can actually move the P&L," is a real finance-reporter test. A has more range, but "Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet" is the kind of confident overreach that gets a founder laughed out of a markets inbox.
gaps_in_A: "Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet" asserts market reaction the update does not provide; make it a question or wait for stock/analyst evidence.
"After Tesla, Rivian opens its charging network to all EVs. The proprietary-charger era is fading" imports a Tesla/network-trend peg and overstates a category shift from one Rivian announcement.
"Tesla opening its Supercharger network was a major structural story; Rivian following is the next chapter" may be useful context, but it is not in the supplied facts and is treated as settled proof.
The revenue angle and investor angle are adjacent; "does this change how Rivian should be valued" needs analyst reaction before it earns its own slot.
gaps_in_B: "Rivian keeps owners cheaper as it opens the gates - the loyalty math of a shared network" is the thinnest angle; it turns one premium-pricing fact into retention theory with no retention data.
"the way it has for one walled competitor" smuggles in an unnamed competitor precedent that was not supplied.
"competitive map of public fast charging (Tesla Supercharger access, Electrify America, the NACS transition)" is useful context, but it needs sourcing before it becomes a pitch frame.
It underplays the cleanest consumer service angle: non-Rivian drivers gained 3,500+ chargers but pay a premium; B mostly routes that through trade positioning instead of driver cost.
